articles.title: Ethereum Devs Set Dec. 15 for Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade
articles.text:
Ethereum devs set Glamsterdam’s Hoodi rollout for mid-December after delays
Glamsterdam’s Hoodi upgrade was delayed in October after concerns that changes to gas pricing could break some existing smart contracts.
Ethereum core developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade for the Hoodi testnet on Dec. 15, nearly two months after it was originally due to go live.
Among a number of upgrades, Glamsterdam changes how much gas Ethereum charges for certain operations under two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. However, testing found that under the new rules, some smart contracts could run out of gas and fail, prompting developers to delay the Hoodi rollout originally set for Oct. 26.
In an All Core Developers Consensus call on Thursday, Ethereum developers set Dec. 15 for Glamsterdam’s activation on the Hoodi testnet. Execution-layer teams reached broad agreement to keep EIP-8037 as written after some developers warned that revising the gas pricing proposal could break other smart contracts and further delay the mainnet rollout.
Ethereum researcher and core developer Ansgar Dietrichs said leaving the question open would have pushed the Hoodi rollout into 2027. “Indecision is also just a decision in itself; it would just mean we delay into the next year,” he said.
Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade made it to the Sepolia testnet on Oct. 6, while Hoodi is the final testnet before it goes to mainnet.
The upgrade aims to advance Ethereum’s layer-1 scaling roadmap with enshrined proposer-builder separation, block-level access lists and changes to gas pricing that better reflect the cost of execution.
Last week, Ethereum Foundation’s Rahul Kothari said mid-January would be the earliest viable date for a mainnet rollout, and that the three projects with the highest-severity compatibility issues had either applied fixes or expected to do so by mid-December.
Some projects with medium-severity issues had given timelines as late as Jan. 10.
Related: Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul

articles.title: What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond
articles.text:
In brief
- Ethereum has completed four major upgrades since the Merge moved it to proof-of-stake in 2022.
- Dencun reduced layer-2 fees, while Pectra and Fusaka expanded scaling and staking.
- Glamsterdam is in testing ahead of a mainnet launch, with Hegotá expected to follow in 2027.
Like all blockchain projects, Ethereum is under active development, with upgrades designed to make it faster, cheaper, and easier to use.
Instead of a single "Ethereum 2.0" event, the network upgrades through coordinated changes called hard forks that introduce new features or modify how the protocol operates.
Since the Merge in September 2022, developers have focused on scaling, lowering transaction costs, improving wallets, and making it easier to run nodes and validators. The Ethereum community is also aiming for roughly two major upgrades per year when research and testing are ready.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Ethereum's rollup-focused scaling strategy
Ethereum's scaling plan relies on layer-2 networks. These are separate blockchains built on top of Ethereum that process transactions off-chain and send results back to Ethereum for security and settlement.
Many layer-2 systems use rollups, which bundle multiple transactions together and post them to Ethereum as a single batch, allowing Ethereum to support more activity without the base chain processing every transaction.
As a result, much of Ethereum's development has focused on making it cheaper and easier for rollups to use the network. More recent upgrades have also aimed to scale Ethereum's base layer directly, by raising the amount of activity each block can hold.
The six phases of the Ethereum roadmap
In July 2022, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin described the network's six roadmap phases as the Merge, the Surge, the Scourge, the Verge, the Purge, and the Splurge.
These phases are not single upgrades but broad goals, and several progress in parallel.
- The Merge: Completed. Ethereum moved from mining to staking, cutting energy use by roughly 99.95%.
- The Surge: Ongoing. Focused on scaling Ethereum so rollups can process more transactions at lower cost.
- The Scourge: Ongoing. Focused on reducing the influence of intermediaries in block production and addressing maximal extractable value (MEV).
- The Verge: Ongoing. Aims to make verifying Ethereum's state far less resource-intensive, moving toward a "stateless" design in which nodes don't need to store all of the network's data.
- The Purge: Ongoing. Focused on pruning old data and simplifying the protocol to make Ethereum easier to maintain.
- The Splurge: A collection of smaller improvements and long-term upgrades that enhance usability and efficiency.
Timeline of Ethereum upgrades
Ethereum's roadmap is implemented through a series of hard forks.
Completed upgrades
- September 2022 — The Merge: Ethereum transitioned from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake, reducing energy use by about 99.95%. Validators now lock up ETH to secure the network. The upgrade changed Ethereum's security mechanism but did not directly lower fees or increase transaction speed.
- April 2023 — Shanghai/Shapella: Shapella enabled validator withdrawals. Early validators had locked ETH for years without a withdrawal option. The upgrade introduced partial withdrawals and full exits.
- March 2024 — Dencun: Dencun introduced proto-danksharding (EIP-4844). It added temporary "blob" storage, creating cheaper space for rollup data so it no longer competes with normal transactions for block space. This significantly reduced costs for many layer-2 networks.
- May 2025 — Pectra: Pectra combined the "Prague" (execution) and "Electra" (consensus) upgrades. Wallet changes such as EIP-7702 allow standard wallets to behave like smart accounts in some cases, enabling features like batching actions into one transaction or delegating gas payment. The upgrade also raised the maximum effective stake per validator from 32 ETH to 2,048 ETH, letting large operators consolidate into fewer validators, which some fear could increase concentration. Pectra also increased Ethereum's capacity to handle rollup data.
- December 2025 — Fusaka: Ethereum's Fusaka hard fork (short for Fulu-Osaka) activated on mainnet in early December 2025 and focused on data availability, including Peer Data Availability Sampling (PeerDAS), which lets validators verify small samples of rollup data instead of downloading all of it. This supports more rollup data per block without requiring much more powerful hardware and is paired with higher data capacity at the protocol level.
Planned and upcoming upgrades
Glamsterdam (in testing)
Glamsterdam is the upgrade after Fusaka, and its name combines "Amsterdam," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devconnect location, and "Gloas," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star. It focuses on scaling Ethereum's base layer, with two headline features:
- Enshrined proposer-builder separation (ePBS, EIP-7732) builds the hand-off between the validators who propose blocks and the builders who assemble them directly into the protocol, removing the need for third-party relays. It extends the time available to spread block data across the network from about 2 seconds to about 9 seconds, allowing much larger blocks.
- Block-level access lists (BALs, EIP-7928) give nodes an upfront map of which data each transaction in a block will touch, so they can process non-overlapping transactions in parallel instead of one by one, and sync faster.
Glamsterdam also raises the gas cost of creating new state, such as accounts and contracts, to target database growth of about 120 GiB a year, and reprices reading stored data, to keep hardware requirements manageable as capacity rises. Under one proposal, EIP-8037, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as before.
Other scheduled changes would make a standard ETH transfer between existing accounts up to 71% cheaper, let developers deploy contracts to the same address across chains, make ETH transfers emit a log that apps can track, raise the maximum contract size from about 24KiB to 64KiB, and speed up validator exits and consolidations.
Node operators and stakers will need to update their clients to support the fork; ETH holders do not need to do anything.
Developers originally targeted the first half of 2026. Glamsterdam went live on the Sepolia testnet in October 2026, but a fork on the Hoodi testnet planned for October 26, 2026, was postponed after security firm ChainSecurity warned that the upgrade's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existing smart contracts.
In November 2026, developers rescheduled the Hoodi fork for December 15, 2026, and agreed to ship the gas changes unaltered. As of November 2026, no mainnet date had been set.
Hegotá (expected in 2027)
Hegotá is the upgrade planned to follow Glamsterdam. Its name combines "Bogotá," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devcon location, and "Heze," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star.
As of its October 2026 update, ethereum.org expected Hegotá on mainnet in the second quarter of 2027, with a fork on the Sepolia testnet to come first, though no dates had been confirmed. Two changes are scheduled for inclusion.
The headliner, Fork-choice Enforced Inclusion Lists (FOCIL, EIP-7805), aims to strengthen censorship resistance by having a committee of validators propose lists of transactions that block builders must include, so that no single party can keep a valid transaction out of a block. Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would let each account set its own rules for what counts as a valid transaction, rather than relying on a single fixed signature scheme. That would bring features such as social recovery, spending limits, multiple approvals and gas sponsorship directly into the protocol, and let accounts adopt signature schemes designed to resist quantum computers.
Dozens of other proposals are being considered, but none are settled, and the rest of Hegotá's scope is still being decided. In November 2026, some developers argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, with a decision on Hegotá's full scope expected in December 2026. Forkcast tracks the live status of each proposal.
Upgrade names and scopes can change during development as proposals are refined before each hard fork.
What Ethereum's upgrades aim to achieve
Ethereum's roadmap continues to evolve as research progresses and upgrades are tested on devnets and testnets before mainnet deployment.
This article was updated in November 2026, and will be amended as as new milestones are confirmed.

articles.title: Crypto Bug Bounty Platforms Are Fighting AI Spam With AI
articles.text:
AI is driving a flood of crypto bug reports. Now it’s helping sort them
Bug bounty platform HackerOne said it’s increasing its triage throughput with AI agents after a record quarter of reports in the third quarter.
Crypto bug bounty platforms have expanded their use of artificial intelligence to keep up with a growing mountain of AI-assisted security reports.
Crypto-focused HackenProof said in October that it was using AI to triage 70% of submissions fully autonomously, aiming to hit 85% by the end of 2026. It said it received an average of about 6,100 bug reports a month in the third quarter, 2.4 times the reports from December last year.
Rival Immunefi last week said submissions to its platform rose 136% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, as it introduced a tool that can flag duplicates before a researcher submits a report.
Bug bounty programs pay independent researchers to find and report potential security flaws. AI has helped researchers uncover more genuine vulnerabilities, but has also swelled the volume of invalid and duplicate submissions, making it harder for security teams to identify the threats that need urgent attention.
It’s like “bringing a sword to a gunfight,” Dmitry Tokarev, founder of crypto wallet provider Bron, told Cointelegraph, referring to security teams that haven’t already adopted AI to sift through reports.
The turning point for AI-assisted bug hunting
Several bug bounty platforms have identified February as a turning point in the surge of AI-assisted vulnerability reports, coinciding with the release of more capable AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6.
HackenProof said Claude Opus 4.6 could work through larger codebases and sustain tasks for longer. HackerOne said the arrival of more capable AI models and tools in that month saw a sudden shift from a “human-only submission environment.”
Some crypto developers are also experimenting with financial disincentives to curb low-quality submissions.
The team behind Firedancer, a Solana validator client developed by Jump Crypto, which also uses AI to screen reports, took an additional measure in October.
To deter spam, it began requiring researchers to burn 1 SOL for each bug report they want considered for a bounty. The token is permanently destroyed, even if the report turns out to be a duplicate.
In a November update published Tuesday, HackerOne’s vice president of operations Tony Lee said they began requiring researchers to verify their identities before submitting reports in the third quarter. It also expanded its triage team and began using AI agents to automatically close clear-cut cases, such as spam and duplicate reports.
In October, it gave customers more control over how many reports their public programs receive.
Related: AI labs likely sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells,’ computer scientist says
Security teams brace for more bug reports and attacks
Lee said he expects vulnerability reports to keep climbing “for the foreseeable future” after recording a 22% increase in report volume in Q3 compared to the previous quarter.
Meanwhile, insurer QBE and risk consultancy Control Risks on Wednesday forecast more disruptive cyber incidents in 2027 across the 14 markets they studied, pointing to the “industrialization of AI” as one of the factors.
Mike Blank, chief product officer at blockchain infrastructure firm R3, also said he expects the number of hacks to rise sharply in 2027, but said crypto teams should pay closer attention to how much damage a single breach can cause, rather than the number of attacks.
“The real difference will be between protocols where a stolen key can drain everything and those where it can only pause operations,” Blank said.

articles.title: Bitcoin privacy weakness links wallet addresses to network nodes in 30 out of 30 tests
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Abubakar Sadiq Ismail reported 30 correct address-to-node matches in 30 attempts on a local Bitcoin test network.
- Watch-only setups can expose the same link because wallets can recognize addresses without holding spending keys.
- An open Bitcoin Core proposal would suppress some repeat announcements, while other rebroadcast privacy risks could remain.
On Nov. 25, researcher Abubakar Sadiq Ismail reported linking addresses to the correct nodes in all 30 attempts in regtest, Bitcoin Core’s local testing environment.
Ismail said the same behavior can expose a watch-only wallet, which monitors addresses and transactions without storing the keys needed to spend the funds.
A service can keep its spending keys off the machine it uses to monitor deposits, and a match identifies the node whose wallet recognizes the address.
In his write-up on wallet rebroadcast for Delving Bitcoin, Ismail described a long-known behavior in Bitcoin Core. After a wallet learns about an unconfirmed transaction, it can announce that transaction again to peers.
That repeated announcement can reveal that the node’s wallet recognizes activity involving a particular address or output. The blockchain records confirmed transactions, while the extra clue about who tracks an address comes from the node’s network activity.
Ismail’s reported matches show that wallet behavior can reveal an address-to-node link in a controlled network.
A node is a computer running software that exchanges information with peers on the Bitcoin network. Its wallet tracks addresses and transactions, and software that loads addresses into a Bitcoin Core wallet can inherit the exposure, even when its role is limited to monitoring.
One node may track two addresses that belong to different users of the same service, and a single operator can also run several nodes. An observer who sees a match learns how a wallet is used, while ownership across those addresses remains uncertain.
What operators can change
An operator can use private broadcast to shield the initial announcement of a transaction. If it stays unconfirmed, Bitcoin Core’s wallet may later announce it more broadly.
A user who chooses a private path for the first announcement can still lose some of that protection in the later broadcast.
Ismail said a node that uses Tor or I2P alongside peers on the public internet can still expose its public IP address. While limiting peers to Tor or I2P can protect the public IP from this rebroadcast, the address may still be associated with the node’s identity on the privacy network.
Ismail pointed to -walletbroadcast=0 as a way to disable wallet-initiated announcements, which also stops the wallet from automatically announcing the user’s own new transactions. Users who turn off wallet broadcasting need a separate way to relay the payments they intend to send.
A pending Bitcoin Core proposal would preserve part of rebroadcast’s original purpose. A pending transaction can drop out of a node’s mempool, its local pool of unconfirmed transactions, and still need another chance to reach the network.
Bitcoin Core pull request #36482 would limit wallet rebroadcast to transactions the node newly accepts into that pool. The wallet could still relay transactions that had dropped out if the node accepts them again.
The proposal opened on Oct. 8, several weeks before Ismail published his results, and remained open on Nov. 27. The Delving Bitcoin discussion points to residual privacy risks even if the change is adopted.
It would suppress repeat announcements for transactions already in a node’s mempool, while other wallet rebroadcasts could still reveal which node recognizes a transaction.

articles.title: Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension Four Weeks After $6.4B Hack
articles.text:
In brief
- Binance said it has completed its withdrawal recovery work and fully lifted the suspension imposed after the October 29 hack.
- Withdrawals on a small number of networks remain paused for maintenance or upgrades, which Binance said is separate from its recovery work.
- North Korea-linked launderers have moved more than $600 million of the stolen crypto through THORChain, researchers estimate, as U.S. authorities work to recover the funds.
Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it imposed after the record $6.4 billion hack of the exchange in October, four weeks after the attack.
"Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted," the exchange said in an announcement on Thursday.
Service Recovery Update:
Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted. Withdrawals are open across nearly all networks. Separately, a small number are temporarily paused due to network maintenance, which… pic.twitter.com/QZmXhsc2qA
— Binance (@binance) November 26, 2026
Withdrawals for a small number of networks are still temporarily paused while they undergo maintenance or planned upgrades, affecting a very small percentage of regular traffic, Binance said. That is separate from its recovery work and part of its standard practice of pausing a network's withdrawals when external conditions require it, the exchange added.
Binance said all user assets remain fully backed, and pointed users to its proof of reserves website, where they can check that their holdings are backed at least 1:1.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BNB with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
The exchange also warned that events like the hack can attract phishing attempts. It said it will never ask users for their passwords, two-factor authentication codes or seed phrases, and will never contact them to "speed up withdrawals," offer "priority processing," or move their assets into a "Binance vault."
Recovering the funds
The FBI has attributed the October 29 attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. North Korea has denied involvement. Binance set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses after the hack, and has won a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts.
Efforts to recover the stolen crypto are ongoing. On Monday, the U.S. Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture action for more than $1.1 billion in USDC stolen in the hack, and said the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto since the attack.
The hackers have continued to move what they still control. More than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through cross-chain exchange THORChain, according to estimates from blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and Elliptic, Reuters reported. Elliptic told the news agency that $342 million has also moved through a Bitcoin coinjoin service, a technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, up from the $247 million it reported earlier this week.
Laundering the funds could take months or even years, but cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea, TRM Labs' global head of policy Ari Redbord told Reuters.
The FBI on October 31 called on crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block addresses linked to the hack. THORChain, which says it does not censor transactions or carry out Know Your Customer checks, may have earned as much as $1 million in fees from the launderers' swaps, according to TRM Labs estimates cited by Reuters.
Why not just shut THORChain down after a hack?@CBarraford's answer to @RBoccius : by his count, 98% of THORChain's volume is legitimate trading. Shut it down and you hit all those people, the ones using it for their own financial freedom.
The hackers would barely notice.… pic.twitter.com/ax7Bwz9Uvu
— THORChain (@THORChain) November 26, 2026
THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford defended the protocol in a video posted by THORChain on Thursday, saying that by his count 98% of its volume is legitimate trading. Shutting it down would hurt those who use the system for "completely neutral and good purposes for their own individual financial freedom and liberty," while barely inconveniencing the hackers, he argued. Bad actors will "find a way to get out just the same, they'll still go through Russian dark net things or Chinese," he said.

articles.title: Monero Delisted by KuCoin as Grayscale Doubles Down on Zcash
articles.text:
Privacy coins face diverging fortunes as KuCoin moves to drop Monero
As KuCoin joins exchanges dropping Monero ahead of new EU restrictions, Grayscale argues that Zcash’s privacy design sets it apart.
Crypto exchange KuCoin said Thursday it will delist Monero (XMR) on Nov. 30, making it the second major platform this month to drop the privacy coin. Exchange MEXC suspended XMR spot trading and delisted its perpetual futures contracts earlier in November.
KuCoin has already suspended XMR deposits and plans to close withdrawals on Dec. 31. XMR fell 10.5% to $449.98 as of 7:00 p.m. UTC on Thursday. The drop extends a decline from about $625 on Nov. 3.
The delisting comes as the European Union prepares to restrict privacy coins on regulated platforms. Starting July 10, 2027, the bloc’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation will prohibit financial firms, including crypto asset service providers, from maintaining anonymous accounts or accounts that obscure transactions through “anonymity-enhancing coins,” regardless of whether the privacy features are enabled by default or optional. The regulation does not prohibit individuals from holding privacy coins in self-custody wallets.
Launched in 2014, Monero conceals transaction amounts and the wallet addresses of senders and recipients by default. Unlike Monero, Zcash (ZEC), launched in 2016, allows users to choose between transparent and shielded transactions. Both cryptocurrencies have faced regulatory scrutiny over the past few years, with Binance delisting Monero in 2024 and Kraken ending support for it in the European Economic Area later that year.
Zach Pandl, head of research at Grayscale, which launched the first US spot ZEC exchange-traded fund (ETF) in August, said Zcash is positioned differently from Monero. He told Cointelegraph that the firm’s commitment to Zcash will continue for “many years to come.”
Delistings mount ahead of EU privacy coin restrictions
KuCoin’s delisting of Monero follows a series of similar moves by crypto exchanges amid growing regulatory pressure on privacy coins. Since 2018, when Japan’s Financial Services Agency pressed exchanges to drop anonymity coins, regulators in other jurisdictions, including South Korea and Dubai, have also taken steps to restrict their use or availability.
In Europe, plans to restrict privacy coins emerged as early as 2022, when a leaked draft of an Anti-Money Laundering bill came to light. The EU’s regulation defines “anonymity-enhancing coins” as cryptocurrencies with built-in features that anonymize transaction data “either systematically or optionally,” which could bring cryptocurrencies with opt-in privacy features, such as Zcash, within the scope of the restrictions.
Related: Bitwise seeks Texas Stock Exchange listing for Zcash ETF
Pandl said that viewing keys allow Zcash holders to disclose transactions “to an auditor or regulator, law enforcement if they need.” He said the feature gives users greater control over who can access their financial information. “That is exactly how the financial system works today. It’s just that it gives the authority to individuals rather than institutions,” he said.
However, whether viewing keys alone can satisfy regulatory requirements remains a point of debate.
Other approaches to privacy are gaining traction among traditional financial institutions looking to use public blockchains. In April, Paris-based digital asset infrastructure provider Dfns partnered with cryptography firm Zama to bring confidential transactions to its more than 400 enterprise clients, including banks, fintechs and custodians. The collaboration uses encryption to conceal transaction amounts and balances on public blockchains while allowing authorized parties to access the information for compliance purposes.
Grayscale says shielding beats obfuscation
Grayscale has offered exposure to ZEC since the launch of its Zcash Trust in 2017, based on the view that transaction privacy would be essential for financial institutions to adopt public blockchains.
Pandl said that as AI has advanced, it has become “much easier to link pseudonymous addresses with offchain information.” Monero, he explained, uses ring signatures that obscure the source of transactions among multiple possible signers, a method Pandl said “may be vulnerable” as AI-powered blockchain analytics improve.
“We believe strongly that Zcash is the stronger tech,” he said, because “it takes a shielding approach rather than an obfuscation approach.” Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs to verify shielded transactions without publicly revealing sensitive transaction data onchain.
Monero developers, however, are working on an upgrade that would replace ring signatures with a zero-knowledge proof system in a bid to enhance transaction privacy.
“For public blockchain technology to become a mainstream part of the financial system, it absolutely needs a privacy layer,” Pandl said.
ETF conviction despite outflows
Grayscale’s Zcash ETF began trading on NYSE Arca on Aug. 25, following the conversion of its Zcash Trust. While investors seeking to use Zcash’s privacy features would need to hold the cryptocurrency directly, “the ETF can provide the store of value use case of these [privacy] technologies,” Pandl said.
Grayscale’s ETF reached $1 billion in assets under management on Sept. 24, but that figure had fallen to $406 million on Wednesday. Zcash more than tripled in value this year, rising to $1,653 on Sept. 26 from $524 on Jan. 1, according to Token Terminal data. Its price more than doubled in the month following the ETF’s launch but has since fallen back to $770. The cryptocurrency remains up about 50% year to date.
Pandl described Zcash’s price appreciation over the past year as “Bitcoin’s Solana moment,” referring to Solana’s growing market cap and its challenge to Ethereum’s dominance as the “leading smart contract platform.”
“At 1.2% of Bitcoin’s market cap, I would still consider Zcash at a relatively low value,” he said, adding that Grayscale has no price targets for ZEC.

articles.title: XRP holders face a choice between earning more yield and getting their tokens back
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Spectra closed its November Firelight pool and listed a February rollover option with about $1.4 million in liquidity.
- Six traced rollovers released about 27,903 stXRP from November liquidity-provider positions and minted new February pool shares.
- Firelight’s direct withdrawal makes FXRP claimable in 30 to 60 days, before a separate redemption can deliver native XRP.
Spectra’s November XRP-linked yield pool closed on Nov. 26, and the platform is offering liquidity providers a rollover into a February Firelight market with about $1.4 million in listed liquidity.
Holders can keep their XRP-linked exposure on Flare or redeem the old position and take the separate steps to get native XRP back.
Spectra’s market overview put the Feb. 19, 2027 pool at $1.43 million and showed a 3.89% indicative fixed annual percentage yield at 10:50 UTC on Nov. 27. By 13:10 UTC, the same overview showed $1.42 million and 3.65%.
In the later snapshot, its December and March Firelight pools had $75,000 and $13,000.
Two-sided liquidity for the three Firelight stXRP maturities in Spectra’s market overview at 13:10 UTC on Nov. 27.
The pools use stXRP, Firelight’s vault share for FXRP deposits, the version of XRP used on Flare, and Spectra pairs those shares with principal tokens that come due on a set date.
What moved into February
Between late Nov. 26 and the morning of Nov. 27, six transactions burned November liquidity-provider tokens and minted February pool shares for the same wallets.
The six November exits released about 27,903 stXRP, including the proceeds from redeeming the principal tokens held in the November pool.
Those rollovers deposited about 13,852 stXRP and 14,120 newly minted principal tokens into the February pool, and the rest of the stXRP went into minting those principal tokens.
A wallet redeemed 111,632 November principal tokens in a separate Flare transaction at 11:31 UTC on Nov. 27, and the transaction routed 111,138 stXRP into the February pool and sent 112,632 February principal tokens back to that wallet.
It purchased the later principal token, leaving the holder with a claim on FXRP at the new maturity.
February principal tokens can be bought at a discount and redeemed for FXRP at maturity, subject to losses in the underlying strategy.
A large order can move the price and secure a different rate, so the liquidity figure alone gives little indication of how much can trade near the displayed rate.
Spectra’s rollover review shows the quoted and worst-case fixed rates for the amount entered, plus the minimum the holder would receive. If a later market cannot offer a positive fixed rate for that amount, Spectra can exclude it and suggest a smaller order. Liquidity providers receive new February pool shares. The November rollover screen showed a 5.41% pool APY around 13:07 UTC, a variable pool return shown separately from the fixed principal-token rate. Both rollovers require the holder to act.
Getting native XRP back
A holder who declines to roll can redeem matured principal tokens for the default stXRP or choose FXRP when offered.
Redeeming a matured pool share first unwinds the position and redeems the principal tokens it held, with the app showing which output is available and how much the holder would receive.
Holders who receive stXRP can swap stXRP at the market price, which can differ from Firelight’s vault value, or request a direct withdrawal.
The direct route stops rewards at the request and makes FXRP claimable in 30 to 60 days under Firelight’s current coverage schedule. A second transaction collects the FXRP, and eligible claims from periods the capital backed can still reduce the payout.
FXRP received from any of those routes is still on Flare, so getting XRP back on its own ledger takes a separate FAssets redemption.
On the standard route, Flare burns the FXRP, and an agent sends native XRP to the holder’s XRP Ledger address after fees by the payment deadline. A holder who redeems directly into FXRP can go straight to that step.
Holders already able to redeem into FXRP can request native XRP without taking on a new maturity or waiting through Firelight’s unstaking window. For holders leaving with stXRP, a market swap avoids the vault’s wait if a usable quote is available.

articles.title: Kalshi Courts Small Businesses With 'Microinsurance' as State Crackdowns Bite
articles.text:
In brief
- About 500 businesses have used Kalshi to hedge risks ranging from commodity price swings to extreme weather and power outages, the prediction market told the Financial Times.
- Kalshi is diversifying beyond sports contracts, which make up most of its trading and face legal challenges in more than 20 states.
- This week, Kalshi pulled out of Utah, prompting the state to move to drop criminal charges against the company and its co-founders.
Prediction market Kalshi is pitching its platform to small businesses as a form of insurance, as legal fights with states over its sports contracts mount.
About 500 businesses have used Kalshi to hedge risks ranging from commodity price swings to extreme weather and power outages, Nicolas Hull, the company's director of business development, told the Financial Times. Hull described the offering as "almost a form of microinsurance," but said almost all of the small businesses he had spoken to had never hedged before.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
One New York rice brand plans to pay about $9,000 for contracts that would pay out up to $60,000 if new tariffs on Indian rice imports hit, according to the FT. A new crop of brokers is using AI tools to find small businesses exposed to regulatory changes, such as tariffs or tax increases, and structure contracts for them to trade.
Event organizers have used the same approach. NEXTPredict, which runs a prediction markets conference, paid a $12,000 premium for Kalshi contracts that would have returned about $3 million if more than half of scheduled arrivals at New York's JFK airport were cancelled the day before its October event, with trading firm Susquehanna taking the other side. The conference went ahead as planned, so the contracts did not pay out.
It is not Kalshi's first attempt to move beyond retail betting. It has also struck a deal with Game Point Capital to enter the sports insurance market.
Liquidity hurdles
The business markets are still small. Kalshi is offering cash incentives to traders to provide enough liquidity for businesses to take part, according to the FT, and insurance broker Lockton told the newspaper it had not yet seen much uptake. Kalshi also turned down a request to hedge wildfire risk, citing its policy against markets that could create "perverse incentives" for traders, the FT reported.
Sports have dominated Kalshi's trading. About 87% of the $39.7 billion traded on the platform in the year to February 2026 was on sports, according to a Congressional Research Service report, and Kentucky has alleged that sports made up 89% of its 2025 volume.
When will Polymarket's POLY TGE?
Legal pressure mounts
Kalshi's diversification push comes amid an escalation in its legal fights this week. The prediction market paused operations in the state on Monday after failing to persuade a federal appeals court to halt Utah's enforcement actions, spokesperson Jacki McGavick told Ars Technica, cutting off what she said were more than 177,000 users.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown's office then moved to dismiss the 14 criminal charges it filed in October against Kalshi and its co-founders, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara, after Kalshi agreed to block users in the state, the office said. The dismissal is without prejudice, meaning the charges can be refiled. Including Kalshi, seven prediction market companies have agreed to stop operating in Utah.
Kalshi has stopped taking bets from Utahns. Utah law treats betting on sports and other events as gambling, and that includes prediction markets. The Office is moving to dismiss its 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and individual defendants, and may refile them if Kalshi takes… pic.twitter.com/vjLJpoynaO
— Office of the Utah Attorney General (@UtahAG) November 24, 2026
"Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges," Brown said. Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth tweeted that "good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized."
Elsewhere, Arkansas has sued Kalshi, and New York's attorney general is seeking $3.6 billion from the company. On Monday, a New York judge denied the state's request for a temporary restraining order that risked shutting Kalshi down nationwide, and urged it to limit bets by users under 21, Scripps News reported. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has invoked emergency powers to keep Kalshi trading there.
Kalshi expects the question of who regulates prediction markets to reach the Supreme Court. So far, three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate the platforms, and one has found they cannot. Meanwhile, the CFTC has set out new rules to separate prediction markets from gambling, and the Senate has passed a bill banning bets on war, terrorism and death.

articles.title: How Coldcard’s $112 million Bitcoin exploit slipped past 15 security reviews
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Coldcard's Bitcoin wallet vulnerability went undetected for five years despite at least 15 independent security research and review efforts.
- Galaxy Research identified 1,778.84 BTC worth $112.7 million stolen from more than 8,600 addresses.
- Despite independently verified firmware fixes, affected owners remain vulnerable until they move their Bitcoin to newly generated wallets.
A security flaw in Coldcard's Bitcoin hardware wallets went undetected for more than five years despite at least 15 independent security research and review efforts.
Coinkite, the wallet's manufacturer, published its postmortem on Nov. 24, detailing how a firmware defect introduced in March 2021 weakened the recovery phrases generated by its devices, enabling attackers to steal customers' Bitcoin without accessing their hardware wallets.
An Aug. 14 analysis by Galaxy Research identified with high confidence 1,778.84 BTC, worth $112.7 million at the time, stolen from more than 8,600 addresses. Galaxy estimated that losses could reach 2,417 BTC, or $153 million, if additional suspected thefts were confirmed.
Coinkite said it had matched approximately 300 loss-related support tickets to 236 customer accounts, representing about 0.2% of its estimated user base. However, the company acknowledged that the actual number of affected customers was likely higher.
How Coldcard's security reviews missed the flaw
The vulnerability originated from a firmware configuration error that caused Coldcard devices to generate recovery phrases using a weaker software-based random number generator instead of the intended hardware component.
The devices continued producing apparently valid recovery phrases, allowing the defect to escape routine security and functionality tests.
Coinkite's postmortem estimates that the defect substantially reduced the randomness protecting recovery phrases across five Coldcard models, including the Mk2, Mk3, Mk4, Mk5 and Q.
Attackers exploited that weakness to reconstruct private keys offline and transfer Bitcoin from affected wallets.
Between 2021 and 2026, Coldcard underwent at least 15 independent security research and review efforts, including two paid third-party product reviews. Its publicly available firmware repository also had 54 contributors.
One commissioned review in March 2022 specifically examined random-number generation and related security measures without discovering the defect.
More recently, independent security researcher Rob Hamilton used OpenAI's Cybersecurity Harness to examine Coldcard's firmware between May 1 and June 26.
The AI-assisted review generated 85 potential security findings, several of which prompted fixes, but failed to identify the seed-generation vulnerability.
A separate June 17 review by security researcher Nick Farrow also examined weak random-number generation and concluded that the relevant implementation was sound.
Coinkite attributed these failures to a gap in its verification process. Existing checks established that the hardware random-number generator was present in the firmware but failed to confirm whether the software actually used it to create recovery phrases.
The company identified the defect on July 30, following the first reported thefts, and released corrected firmware the following day.
Why some Coldcard owners still need to move their Bitcoin
Security firm Keylabs subsequently verified the fix across four firmware releases for Coldcard's Mk5 and Q wallets.
Coinkite has also introduced additional safeguards that combine user-provided randomness with multiple hardware sources when generating new recovery phrases.
However, these changes cannot strengthen recovery phrases created using the defective firmware, leaving previously affected wallets exposed even after their owners install the latest updates.
Coinkite said wallets using securely generated external recovery phrases were unaffected. Owners who incorporated at least 50 fair, independent and private dice rolls during their original wallet setup also remained protected if they followed the prescribed procedure.
The company advises other affected users to generate new recovery phrases using verified firmware and transfer their Bitcoin to the resulting wallets.
Meanwhile, law enforcement continues investigating the thefts, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has opened a separate case.
Coinkite has appealed to whoever controls the stolen Bitcoin to return the funds. Nearly four months after the exploit, however, the company has yet to decide whether it will compensate affected customers.

articles.title: Ethereum Sets December 15 Date for Delayed Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade
articles.text:
In brief
- Ethereum developers scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi testnet for December 15, 2026, at 19:12 UTC, after postponing it in October over security concerns.
- Execution layer teams agreed to ship EIP-8037, the gas change behind the delay, without modifications, despite some concerns about potential breakage.
- No mainnet date has been set. Developers also deferred a decision on whether to keep FOCIL as a headline feature of Hegotá, the following upgrade.
Ethereum developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi test network for December 15, 2026, more than a month after security concerns forced them to call off the fork.
The upgrade will activate on Hoodi at 19:12 UTC that day, at epoch 143,616, developers agreed during an All Core Devs Consensus (ACDC) call on Thursday, according to an AI-generated summary of the meeting and notes from tracker EIPsInsight. They chose December 15 over December 16.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Client teams on both the execution and consensus layers are expected to cut releases for the fork by early next week.
The upgrade has already gone live on Sepolia, another Ethereum test network, where it began producing blocks in October with a gas limit more than three times mainnet's. Developers have not yet set a date for mainnet.
ETH price on November 29, 4:59PM UTC
Gas changes go ahead unaltered
The Hoodi fork was originally due on October 26, but developers postponed it after security firm ChainSecurity warned that Glamsterdam's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existingsmart contracts, citing 13 real-world examples.
At the center of the concerns is EIP-8037, which raises the cost of creating new data on Ethereum to slow the growth of the network's state, the data every node must store, as block gas limits rise. It also meters that cost separately from other computation, which allows gas to be returned to a contract during execution, something some existing contracts' security checks do not expect.
After reviewing feedback from execution layer clients, developers reached rough consensus on Thursday to ship EIP-8037 as is, rather than delay the upgrade further or change the specification, though some participants raised concerns about potential breakage and the usefulness of the GAS opcode, which reports how much gas remains in a transaction.
Under the proposal, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as it does today, and deploying a 24 kB contract about eight times as much. Its authors said the change would cap state growth at a target of about 120 GiB a year at a 150 million gas limit.
Consensus layer teams also agreed on a fix for how they validate blocks from builders, picking a less disruptive option that most teams considered a stopgap over a cleaner solution that would have required a consensus-breaking change.
Hegotá scope still open
Developers did not decide whether to keep FOCIL, a proposal designed to make it harder for block builders to censor transactions, as a headline feature of Hegotá, Ethereum's next upgrade after Glamsterdam.
Some participants argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, while others said both could be developed in parallel. FOCIL keeps its status as a headline feature until the next ACDC call, around December 10, when developers expect to decide Hegotá's full scope.
Developers agreed to give post-quantum and AI security threats higher priority, at what the summary described as a "DEFCON 2-3" level of urgency. The Ethereum Foundation has said AI posed a more urgent threat to the network than quantum computing.

articles.title: Google’s lightweight Gemini matched two top models on a chemistry test
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Google DeepMind released Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity to help Gemini analyze measurements from tandem mass spectrometry.
- All three Gemini models scored about 97% with internet access and the tools on compounds with public reference spectra.
- The software can narrow candidate structures when a library match is unavailable, and chemists still need to confirm genuinely new structures.
Google DeepMind released tools for interpreting mass spectrometry data in its Antigravity AI platform on Nov. 25. In the company’s test, the software helped its lightweight Gemini 3.8 Flash match two frontier models at identifying known compounds. With the tools and internet access, all three identified the exact molecule in about 97% of attempts on a set of 100 compounds whose fragment patterns were already recorded in public libraries.
The models were farther apart with internet access alone. In DeepMind’s benchmark, Flash missed more than three quarters of its attempts to identify a compound, while Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon missed roughly a quarter to a third. All three scored below 4% with neither internet access nor the specialist tools.
DeepMind drew the test spectra from the Enamine REAL collection in the public MoNA library. The compounds’ structures were also cataloged in PubChem. The team screened out recordings in which the molecule had produced too few useful fragments. The benchmark ran three attempts per spectrum. Runs that took more than an hour counted as failures, while temporary infrastructure and quota errors were excluded.
Tandem mass spectrometry measures the charged fragments a molecule breaks into. To identify the molecule, a chemist can compare that pattern with a reference spectrum recorded from a known compound.
For the internet-only runs, DeepMind said scripts written on the fly struggled with noisy peaks and with choosing which masses to search. The new Mass Spec Skills give Antigravity established software to clean up a signal, look for matching reference spectra and check whether a proposed structure fits the measured fragments.
DeepMind also reported that adding the skills reduced the number of tokens each model generated per attempt, with the largest proportional drop for Flash. Flash with the tools was more accurate than either frontier model with internet access alone.
What the software can do without a spectral-library search
In a test without a spectral-library search, Antigravity used fragment measurements to infer a formula and narrow down candidate structures in PubChem. The compound it selected was already cataloged.
For a compound that is genuinely new, a predicted formula and explanations for some of the peaks can give a chemist a starting point. DeepMind says some structures, including mirror-image molecules, break apart in such similar ways that telling them apart can take another kind of lab measurement.

articles.title: Bitcoin dodged one risk from Japan and now faces a Monday reckoning
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Tokyo inflation excluding fresh food rose to 2.9% in November, while the measure also excluding energy eased to 2.5%.
- The yen weakened against the dollar, lowering the dollar cost of repaying a fixed, unhedged yen balance.
- Monday’s two-year Japanese bond auction gives traders a chance to watch for higher short-term yields alongside a stronger yen.
The yen slipped against the dollar on Friday, cutting the dollar cost of repaying fixed, unhedged yen loans for traders who borrowed the currency to buy Bitcoin. Bitcoin held above 60,000 USDT on Binance during Tokyo trading as two measures of the city's November inflation moved in opposite directions. Monday's two-year government bond auction is the next chance to see whether the yen and short-term yields move higher together.
The Statistics Bureau of Japan said preliminary consumer prices across Tokyo's 23 wards rose 2.9% from a year earlier excluding fresh food, up from 2.6% in October. When energy is also excluded, inflation slowed to 2.5% from 2.6%. The preliminary Tokyo figures offer an early read ahead of the national release.
Electricity and city gas explain much of the split. Electricity prices rose 9.5% from a year earlier, up from 1.7% in October, and city gas prices rose 13.7%, up from 4.9%. Energy's contribution to the headline inflation rate increased by 0.34 percentage points. The overall rate rose more modestly, to 2.8% from 2.7%, as other categories offset part of that increase. The bureau put the increase in electricity's contribution at 0.22 percentage points, and city gas at 0.11.
The dollar bought 159.28 to 159.30 yen at 9 a.m. Friday and 159.33 to 159.35 yen at 5 p.m., according to the Bank of Japan's Friday quotes. That compared with 159.16 to 159.18 yen at 5 p.m. Thursday. Both quotes use Tokyo time.
CoinGlass’s daily Binance data showed Bitcoin trading as low as 60,472 USDT on Nov. 27 as of 11:54 a.m. UTC. CryptoSlate's Bitcoin price tracker put it at $61,529 as of 11:57 a.m. UTC on Friday.
Ahead of the release, the risk for yen-funded Bitcoin trades was that hotter inflation could push the currency and short-term yields higher. An investor who borrows yen to buy Bitcoin and leaves the currency risk unhedged has to buy yen back to repay the loan. When the yen strengthens, the investor needs more dollars to repay the same yen balance even if Bitcoin's dollar price stands still. Friday's weaker yen moved that cost in the other direction.
Interest costs move on a different timetable. A trader pays more in interest if a yen loan has to be replaced at a higher rate. The actual rate and the timing depend on the instrument, maturity and any hedge, so traders with similar Bitcoin positions can face different costs.
What to watch at Monday's auction
Japan's Ministry of Finance has scheduled the November 30 two-year bond auction notice for 10:30 a.m. Tokyo time and the public result for 12:35 p.m. At October’s two-year auction, the yield at the weighted-average accepted price was 1.91%, giving traders a benchmark for the new issue.
The auction yield measures the return implied by the price paid for the new bonds. The two-year yield in secondary trading just before and after the result can show whether investors are repricing the path of Japanese rates. If that market yield rises while the yen strengthens against the dollar, borrowers who need to refinance could face dearer loans just as their outstanding yen debt becomes more expensive in dollars. If yields rise and the yen stays weak, the signals would still be split.
Even a move in both markets would leave open how many Bitcoin positions use yen funding. Bank for International Settlements researchers documented how hard it was to size the broader currency carry trade after the August 2024 unwind.

articles.title: XT Exchange at Eight: Building One Platform, Not More Destinations
articles.text:
Sponsored content. This article is brought to you by XT Exchange.
Where XT stands in 2026
Eight years after launching in 2018, XT Exchange is advancing a broader vision for digital finance. An established international trading business now provides the foundation for expansion across onchain trading strategies, traditional-market exposure, prediction markets and everyday payments.
At the center of this development is a consistent brand promise: “Xplore Crypto, Trade with Trust.” Product development, market education and community engagement give that promise a practical expression, connecting access to financial markets with opportunities to understand and participate in them.
Four priorities define this direction:
Global Scale & Market Access: Building on an international user base and an established spot and derivatives business to expand the range of markets available to eligible users.
Innovation & Practical Utility: Bringing emerging trading approaches and digital-asset applications into a familiar exchange environment.
Education & Community: Maintaining a sustained commitment to market discussion, knowledge sharing and direct engagement with users.
Trust & Long-Term Development: Supporting continued expansion through transparency initiatives, security programs and lasting relationships with clients and partners.
Scale
XT Exchange marks eight years of development with more than 12 million registered users across over 200 countries and regions. This international presence provides the foundation for an expanding platform spanning crypto trading, broader financial markets and digital payments.
As of late October 2026, XT appears among the top ten derivatives exchanges on Coingecko by open interest, with more than 800 perpetual markets and a set of dated futures tracked. An extensive spot marketplace complements that presence: at the same date, Coingecko tracked more than 600 assets and 670 spot trading pairs on the exchange.
During 2026, XT broadened the platform through Hyperliquid Smart Money Copy Trading, an expanding TradFi offering, prediction markets through XPredict and merchant payments through XT Pay. As XT enters a ninth year, that combination gives substance to the ambition expressed through “Build the NeXT.”
A Renewed Identity
The current phase of development follows a comprehensive brand and interface renewal introduced in September 2025. An updated visual identity, redesigned app and web experiences, and improvements to navigation and localization established a more consistent expression of XT across markets and languages.
That identity now connects an increasingly broad range of interactions. Trading, educational discussions, community gatherings and payment applications all contribute to how users encounter XT. The eighth-anniversary theme, “Build the NeXT,” carries this direction forward.
One Account, Not Another Destination
The thread running through XT’s 2026 product work is a simple one: people should not have to run between products. When a new kind of demand appears, XT’s approach is to bring it into the account a user already has rather than send them to a separate venue.
Hyperliquid Smart Money Copy Trading is the clearest example. Introduced in August 2026, the feature connects selected Hyperliquid trader profiles with XT’s futures copy trading environment. Eligible users can discover trading approaches originating on a decentralized venue and follow them through an existing XT account, with copied trades executed within XT.
XPredict applies the same principle to prediction markets, powered by Polymarket. Users can take positions on real-world outcomes with the funds already in their XT account.
XT TradFi brings USDT-settled derivatives referencing currencies, precious metals, equities, indices and commodities into the same futures interface as crypto. These instruments broaden market coverage while retaining the distinction between derivative exposure and ownership of an underlying asset. Development continued throughout 2026, with additional currency-pair contracts announced in September and nine further contracts on October 29. The RWA Zone, introduced in November 2025, adds a dedicated destination for exploring tokenized-asset projects.
Through XT Pay’s Scan to Pay, eligible users can fund supported merchant purchases with USDT held in an XT account, with payment partners handling local settlement. Availability varies by user, location, merchant and service partner. In supported markets, the service turns a balance someone already holds into a way to pay for something they need.
Each of these additions is judged by the same test: does it make the whole XT experience easier, or only longer?
Nearly Two Years of Weekly Roundtables
For nearly two years, XT has hosted a weekly roundtable, making market education a sustained commitment to the community. Week after week, these conversations take up the questions shaping digital finance, from macroeconomic developments and capital flows to emerging technologies and risk awareness.
Published discussions have explored connections between gold, technology stocks and crypto, as well as the interpretation of spot demand, derivatives activity and market risk. Recaps and recordings extend the conversations beyond the live sessions, building a continuing resource for users navigating changing markets.
Users encounter XT as a place to explore markets, exchange perspectives and develop understanding alongside participation. Nearly two years of weekly programming makes that commitment visible through sustained action.
Transparency That Can Be Checked
“Trade with Trust” is supported by mechanisms users can examine. The XT Proof of Reserves program provides reserve disclosures and balance verification for assets within the reporting scope, and a public bug bounty program on HackenProof, active since 2023, gives external security researchers a standing channel to report vulnerabilities.
Built Through Relationships
Community engagement extends beyond the trading platform. XT’s 2025 recap documents gatherings in Hong Kong, Vietnam, Rwanda and Istanbul. In 2026, an eighth-anniversary gathering in Singapore on October 7 brought together clients and partners to recognize shared progress and look toward the next stage of development.
Alongside weekly educational programming, these gatherings reflect a continuing investment in relationships. Global reach takes shape through local participation, regular dialogue and sustained connections with the people behind the platform’s activity.
The Next Chapter
Eight years of operation and a substantial international user base support the next stage of expansion. The additions of 2026, from onchain trader discovery and prediction markets to traditional-market exposure and merchant payments, share one purpose: a single account that keeps up with what its owner wants to do. “Build the NeXT” is the name for that work. For XT, the next chapter is about connecting more people with markets, knowledge and practical uses for digital assets, inside a platform built to carry them.
About XT Exchange
Founded in 2018, XT Exchange is a global digital asset trading platform serving more than 12 million registered users across over 200 countries and regions. Its services span spot, margin and futures trading, TradFi market exposure, a real-world asset marketplace, and everyday payments through XT Pay. Guided by Xplore Crypto, Trade with Trust, XT Exchange enters its ninth year with Build the NeXT, reflecting its focus on trust, broader market access and practical uses for digital assets.

articles.title: Australia passes bill that would let people sue AI chatbot providers
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Australia’s Parliament passed a bill giving people a route to sue covered chatbot providers over a breach that caused loss or damage.
- The duty and private right to sue are due to start 12 months after Royal Assent.
- A court could award damages, grant an injunction or order an apology if a claim succeeds.
Australia’s Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care bill on Nov. 25, giving people a future route to sue covered AI chatbot providers over loss or damage caused by a breach of the new online safety duty. Both the duty and the right to sue are due to take effect 12 months after Royal Assent.
The Nov. 25 vote completed the bill’s passage through Parliament. Schedule 2 of Australia’s Digital Duty of Care bill sets out the safety duty and the private right of action. The Senate committee’s report sets out the transition period for that schedule. The communications department confirmed on Nov. 27 that the duty would start 12 months after Royal Assent.
A different part of the bill follows an earlier timetable. Schedule 1, including expanded powers for the eSafety Commissioner over apps and websites used to generate fake nude material, is due to take effect the day after Royal Assent.
What a Digital Duty of Care claimant would need to show
Section 28D covers providers of services that use an internet carriage service to generate material with AI. That brings covered AI chatbots within the scope of the private court remedy. The provision also names social media services, relevant electronic services and designated internet services.
A claimant would need to show that the provider failed to comply with its safety duty and that the failure caused their loss or damage. The bill treats that connection as established if the breach substantially contributed to the loss or damage.
The duty requires providers to take appropriate safety measures, including effective steps to address the risks they identify in their assessments. The explanatory memorandum, quoted by the Senate committee, says a harmful interaction does not necessarily establish a breach. The provider’s response to reasonably foreseeable risks matters, including whether it put effective safeguards in place and kept them working.
If a claim succeeds, the court could award damages, including for emotional distress, issue an injunction or order the provider to apologize. The bill gives courts discretion to choose a remedy suited to the circumstances.
The time limit for bringing a claim is tied to the claimant’s age and the date they suffered the loss or damage. Under section 28E, proceedings must begin before the later of their 21st birthday or six years after the day they suffered the loss or damage.
For someone who is already 21 when they suffer the loss, the six-year period gives the later date. For someone who suffers loss or damage as a child, the 21st birthday can be the later date, depending on their age when they suffered the loss.

articles.title: Bank of England to test how UK finance would recover from an AI disruption
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The Bank of England plans a voluntary 2027 stress test involving a disruption linked to frontier AI.
- A weakness at a shared provider could disrupt several firms at once and reveal gaps in how the sector recovers.
- The Bank plans testing in summer 2027 and aims to publish findings on common themes in the fourth quarter.
The Bank of England will use a frontier AI scenario in its 2027 operational stress test to see how a disruption involving advanced AI could affect UK finance. One question is whether firms’ recovery plans would work together if several institutions faced disruption at once. The voluntary, exploratory exercise will examine both individual firms and the wider sector.
The Bank set out the plan for its Cyber and Operational Resilience Stress Test in its Nov. 26 Financial Stability Report. It is discussing possible scenarios with firms, industry groups and technical experts. The Bank plans to invite suitable participants for testing in summer 2027 and publish findings on common themes in the fourth quarter.
What one firm’s test can miss
The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee record warned that a weakness at a common supplier could disrupt several firms and financial market infrastructure at once. A firm can test how quickly it would restore its own operations. The committee said risks can remain across the system even when individual firms have credible fallbacks. A Solana routing outage showed how a shared provider can disrupt independently run infrastructure. Validators representing about 29% of stake stopped voting when one provider’s routing failed.
In its wider resilience work, the Bank is examining whether firms’ workarounds can collectively sustain a minimum level of activity in retail and wholesale payments and sterling interest-rate markets. In those markets, a priority is keeping settlement of UK government bond trades running. That work illustrates the stakes of joint recovery while the Bank weighs scenarios for the AI exercise.
The Bank says a prolonged interruption to retail payments could leave households and businesses unable to make or receive essential payments. In wholesale payments, disruption could tie up cash and collateral and leave firms unsure when incoming payments will arrive, putting pressure on other obligations.
An October survey by the Bank and the Financial Conduct Authority shows where firms already rely on the same providers. The three largest cloud and computing providers accounted for 79% of reported relationships in that category. The three largest providers of model access and hosting accounted for 54% of reported relationships in theirs.
The survey also found that adoption of AI agents was widespread among respondents and broad autonomy was rare. Among firms that answered the respective questions in the full survey, 80% said they had deployed AI agents and 2% said they had deployed agents with broad autonomy.
The Bank’s stress-test program includes a separate 2026 exercise on disruption involving a cloud provider and third parties, with findings planned for summer 2027.

articles.text:
